10798-paths-of-glory-impressions-of-war-:
Irvin S. Cobb wrote Paths of Glory from firsthand impressions of the fall and early winter of 1914. He was then on staff service for the Saturday Evening Post in the western theatre of the European War. Dedicated to Major Robert Cobb of Cobb's Kentucky Battery, the book takes its title from Thomas Gray. Cobb tried to write war as he saw it, while memory stayed fresh.

The chapters do not follow campaign order; they form a sequence of pictures of soldiers, refugees, and ruined towns. Cobb's eye for detail and his American voice carry the book. Readers get war reporting at its most immediate, from the opening months of the First World War.
11410-wanderings-in-wessex-an-exploratio:
Edric Holmes's Wanderings in Wessex, an exploration of the southern realm from Itchen to Otter, introduces travelers to one of England's fairest quarters, with twelve full-page drawings by M. M. Vigers and over a hundred text illustrations by the author. Chapters cover Winchester and central Hampshire, Southampton Water and the New Forest, Poole, Wimborne and Purbeck, Dorchester, Weymouth and Portland, west Dorset, east Devon, and the Somerset, Devon, and Dorset borderland.

Holmes apologizes only for brevity, claiming equality with predecessors in affection for Wessex. His object is introduction, not exhaustive treatment. The book suits Hardy readers and walkers, pairing history, lore, and landscape in a single portable volume.
20822-the-camp-fire-girls-on-the-march-o:
Hard feeling from the camp next door sours a stay in Bessie King's Test of Friendship. Jane L. Stewart, in this 1914 Camp Fire Girls tale, has Bessie reflect that things ended well. Had rival girls had their way, no pleasant memory would remain.

Camp Fire Girls, a real movement for American girls, fills these tales with hikes and service. Bessie King leads her friends through tests of loyalty and nerve. The march of the title brings outdoor trials and tests of character. Stewart's set shows how fiction spread the Camp Fire ideals of health, work, and outdoor joy.
22479-the-psychical-researcher-s-tale-th:
J. D. Beresford wrote The Psychical Researcher's Tale, subtitled The Sceptical Poltergeist. It appeared in the New Decameron among tales of mixed kinds. Beresford's researcher investigates a household troubled by a poltergeist.

Cases of the type reach back to John Wesley's days, he notes. The Slippertons kept a fat, very stupid cook at the house. The researcher suspected her of being an unconscious medium for the disturbances. The family, though, were attached to her and refused his advice. They would not give her notice, as he strongly urged. That deadlock gives the tale its comic, sceptical edge. Readers get ghost-hunting told with wit rather than terror.
25454-introduction-of-the-locomotive-saf:
John H. White, associate curator at the Smithsonian's Museum of History and Technology, traces the locomotive safety truck. Early American railroads were cheap and hasty, with rough track, steep grades, and sharp curves. Derailments were a major cause of wrecks, and the safety truck was meant to lead the bobbing locomotive around curves. It came before the steel rail, the automatic coupler, and the airbrake.

White follows the Bissell two-wheel truck, which found wider use in Europe before 1870. American roads clung to the 4-4-0 engine until heavier Mogul and Consolidation types spread, and then the two-wheel truck became common. The Hudson-Bissell truck let those freight engines run, as figures from Meyer's Modern Locomotive Construction show. The paper appeared in Smithsonian Bulletin 228 in 1961.
25618-the-second-battalion-royal-dublin-:
Majors C. F. Romer and A. E. Mainwaring write this regimental history of the Second Battalion, Royal Dublin Fusiliers, in the South African War, with a description of operations in the Aden hinterland. The Duke of Connaught, colonel in chief of the regiment, fronts the book in a portrait.

The narrative follows one battalion through campaign service, marches, and fighting, in the detailed style of a regimental record. Officers' names, places, and dates anchor each phase, and the Aden section extends the story beyond South Africa to a second theatre of imperial service.
2632-the-lights-of-the-church-and-the-li:
Thomas Henry Huxley opens this sixth essay from Science and Hebrew Tradition with three ways of regarding any account of past events. A narrative may be exactly true, with words taken in their natural sense and read by the rules of grammar. Or it may be true in some looser way, or not true at all.

Huxley applies the test to church histories and to scientific claims alike, demanding that each be judged by the same standard. His argument is patient, logical, and quietly devastating. The essay remains a clear guide to weighing testimony, and to telling honest history from pious story.
27663-original-sonnets-on-various-subjec:
Anna Seward published these original sonnets on various subjects, with odes paraphrased from Horace, in London in 1799, printed for G. Sael in the Strand. The price was six shillings and sixpence, and the book was entered at Stationers' Hall.

Seward's preface defends her sonnets: with only nine exceptions out of a hundred, they are strictly sonnets. The nine vary only in rhyming three times, instead of four, in the first part. She refuses the loose elegies of twelve alternate rhymes closing with a couplet that merely assume the sonnet's name. Her frontispiece invites bright Imagination to relume its orient lamp.
cantillon-essai-commerce-1755-fr:
Richard Cantillon's Essai sur la nature du commerce en général appeared in 1755, in French, after his death. No public-domain English translation exists in this entry's line, so the text stands in French. Cantillon, an Irish banker in Paris, wrote the first systematic treatise on economics, before Adam Smith.

Cantillon traced value to land and labor, followed money through an economy, and pictured trade as a flow between town and country. His portrait of the entrepreneur, who buys at known prices and sells at unknown ones, still defines the word's use in economics. Smith and later writers drew on him quietly. The Essai earns its place as the quiet start of economic science.
doe-osti-2588687-artificial-intelligence:
Zhihong Lin of the University of California, Irvine, led this final report for award DE-SC0023640, covering September 2022 through August 2025. The project integrated FRNN, an artificial intelligence and deep learning prediction and control package, into the real-time plasma control system of the DIII-D tokamak.

The hard problem is speed. First-principles instability analysis is too slow for real-time control, so the team built a surrogate. Their SGTC code, derived from the global gyrokinetic code GTC, supplies detailed instability physics. Deep learning models train on it to form a synthetic plasma simulator fast enough to run inside the control loop. Measured signals such as electron cyclotron emission imaging feed the system, supplemented by synthetic SGTC data. Published results include deep learning reconstruction of the tokamak safety factor profile. Fusion transfer learning also rebuilt nonlinear kink mode structures from limited simulation data.
doe-osti-2999176-measurement-of-close-in:
Richard Robey, Andrew Wright, Alfred Cochrane and the PE1 experiment team report in SAND2025-12503, printed October 2025, on listening closely to an underground blast. Shot A of the Low Yield Nuclear Monitoring Physics Experiment 1 series went off at the Nevada National Security Site. The chemical explosion gave ground truth for models that read distant signals and judge what happened below ground. Sensors sat at scaled distances from 70 to 1,000 metres per kiloton.

Measuring so near an explosion is brutal on instruments, since the ground itself heaves. The team designed rugged sensor modules, shock-tested them for burial, and shielded the data system from the shaking. Collection succeeded at a 99 percent rate, and buried instruments kept answering after the shot. Fitted gear inside the tunnel drift also survived. The installed base will serve later PE1 shots, and the data will test computer models of near and far signals.
doe-osti-3015081-solutions-for-lasting-v:
Community energy projects were funded and then cut short in the SOLVE IT Prize final technical report, NLR/TP-6A50-96116, dated January 2026, by Holly and Sweet. The prize paid local organizations to find energy solutions fitted to their own places, awarding 3,740,000 dollars across two completed phases.

Phase 1, Embark, gave 28 winners 80,000 dollars each to name a region, a local challenge, and an engagement plan. Phase 2, Engage, had teams build the vision for their project with local stakeholders. Phase 3, Establish, was planned but never ran, because the competition was terminated in April 2025. Winner sketches range from Delta County, Colorado mine land reuse to Port Sulphur, Louisiana, where a coastal indigenous community sought to protect its way of life.
doe-osti-3375573-development-monitoring-:
A CRADA final report numbered LBNL-2001743, dated February 18, 2026, covers DEMO-FTES, a plan to store heat in cracked rock deep underground. Yingqi Zhang of Lawrence Berkeley Lab was the technical contact. Partners were Jeffrey Burghardt at Pacific Northwest, Matthew Ingraham at Sandia, and Brice Lecampion at EPFL in Lausanne. The idea is simple to state. Pump hot fluid into a fracture web, let the rock soak up the heat, then pull the heat back out months later.

The field test reuses the fracture web made by the EGS Collab project. Old data from a 2022 heat loop run tuned the team's model. With no new wells allowed, the team tried load and unload spans on the wells at hand. One strong case loads for fifty days and unloads for fifty. Well TU serves as the injector in that scheme. A full design report is set to follow this summary.
doe-osti-3917640-analysis-of-natural-gas:
Argonne analysts Thomas H. Coleman, Prakash Thimmapuram, and Saurajyoti Kar study a planned natural gas pipeline link in Puerto Rico in report ANL-26/52, dated July 2026. The link would run from San Juan to Palo Seco, two power hubs on the island's north coast. The work comes from the lab's Decision and Infrastructure Sciences division.

The team tests how the link would change the island's power supply. Tables list the plants and units in play, among them the FEMA emergency generators at Central San Juan, with their fuels and rated sizes. Scenario runs then compare a base case with cases where gas reaches Palo Seco, showing which units burn which fuel. The point is to give planners hard numbers on cost, fuel use, and backup strength before pipe is laid.
durkheim-division-travail-social-1893-fr:
Émile Durkheim published De la division du travail social in 1893, in French. The work was his doctoral thesis and the first major statement of his thought. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in its original language.

Durkheim argued that the division of labor does more than make goods: it binds society together. Older societies held by likeness, he said, while modern ones hold by difference and mutual need. He called those bonds mechanical and organic solidarity. The thesis founded his career and helped make sociology a science of its own, with society itself, not the lone person, as its object.
durkheim-formes-elementaires-1912-fr:
Émile Durkheim published Les Formes élémentaires de la vie religieuse in 1912, in French. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in its original language. The book, on the elementary forms of religious life, was his deepest work on religion and society.

Durkheim studied totemism among Aboriginal peoples of Australia, which he took as religion's simplest form. He argued that when a clan worships its totem, it is really worshipping itself as a society. The sacred, then, is society pictured in symbols. That claim founded the sociology of religion and still drives debate on ritual, symbols, and the ties that hold groups together.
durkheim-regles-methode-1895-fr:
Émile Durkheim published Les Règles de la méthode sociologique in 1895, in French. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in French. The short book is a manifesto: it tells the new science of sociology how it must work if it wants to be a science at all.

Durkheim's first rule was to treat social facts as things, as real as rocks or weather, and to study them from outside. Customs, laws, and beliefs press on each person whether we like them or not. He set rules for proof, comparison, and the sorting of normal from sick societies. The manifesto gave the field its method and its confidence.
durkheim-suicide-1897-fr:
Émile Durkheim published Le Suicide in 1897, in French, a study of suicide built on official statistics. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in French. Durkheim chose a topic that seemed the most private act of all, to prove that society shapes even it.

Rates of suicide, he showed, stayed steady for each group yet differed sharply by faith, family, and social tie. He sorted suicides into types, including the egoistic and the altruistic, each tied to how strongly society held the person. The work founded quantitative sociology, the use of numbers to prove that social facts are real forces in human lives.
nasa-tm-19630012631-a-study-of-cryopump-:
J. O. Ballance, W. K. Roberts, and D. W. Tarbell of Marshall wrote this study on June 27, 1962. It treats cryopumps, pumps that freeze gas onto very cold surfaces. The setting is free molecular flow, where air is too thin to flow smoothly. Ground test chambers use such pumps to mimic space vacuum.

The abstract begins with the share of gas a cold surface can catch. A Monte Carlo computer method modeled how molecules strike and stick. Shape matters: a well-aimed cold trap catches far more gas. The team compared layouts to find which shapes focus molecules best. Better vacuum chambers meant truer tests of spacecraft before flight.
nasa-tm-19690016178-predicted-and-actual:
Thomas J. Karras and Ralph E. Taylor wrote this Goddard preprint, numbered X-560-69-147, comparing predicted and actual spacecraft radio interference. A craft's own circuits can spray radio noise into its telemetry stream home. The team made a first attempt to check interference forecasts against what tracking stations observed and what data teams recovered.

They studied three November 1968 days for the IMP-F spacecraft and examined ten recorded station tapes. A high degree of match was found, with interference verified in eight of the ten tapes. About three percent of the craft's telemetry data was badly degraded, they report. A small share was lost outright, and the rest arrived in poor shape.
nasa-tm-19720020239-detection-of-interpl:
T L Cline and colleagues reported these electron detections in a NASA preprint numbered X-666-72-221. Spacecraft found a quiet time flow of electrons between the planets. Their energies sat above the solar wind's and below true cosmic rays. The energy spectrum fell steadily across the measured range. It spanned from eighteen thousand to nearly two million electron volts. One bump in the spectrum drew special attention.

That feature sat between one hundred and three hundred thousand electron volts. The paper's first part asks where such electrons come from. Finding a steady background flow changed ideas about interplanetary space. Even in quiet times, the space between planets is not empty of energetic particles. The authors weighed solar and planetary sources for the flow.
paths-of-glory-impressions-of-war-writte:
Irvin S. Cobb went to Europe in the fall of 1914 as a war correspondent for The Saturday Evening Post. His Paths of Glory collects the impressions he wrote at and near the front during the first three months of the war. A note dated January 1915 explains that he wrote each piece while the memory was fresh.

The chapters move through Belgium, Germany, France, and England as pictures rather than a strict campaign history. Titles include "To War in a Taxicab" and "Being a Guest of the Kaiser." It is first-hand reporting from the war's opening, by one of America's best-known journalists.
proudhon-confessions-revolutionnaire-185:
P.-J. Proudhon told his own story in Les Confessions d'un revolutionnaire, printed in French in 1851. The revolutionary's confession mixes autobiography with theory. Proudhon had sat in the assembly during the February Revolution of 1848. His narrative runs from that hopeful rising to the coup that crushed the republic.

He explains his famous claims on property and his clashes with rivals and rulers. Prison and exile marked the path his confession records. No public domain English translation exists, so the French text stands alone. Readers meet the first self named anarchist in his own words. The book is both a life and a brief for his cause.
quesnay-oeuvres-economiques-philosophiqu:
Auguste Oncken edited the complete economic and philosophical works of Francois Quesnay in 1888. Quesnay, doctor to the French king, founded the physiocratic school of economics. His Tableau economique, a famous diagram of how wealth flows, leads the system. Land and farming stand at its source, in his scheme.

The French edition gathers his essays, dialogues, and maxims in one critical volume. No public domain English translation exists, so the French original stands as the record. Physiocracy shaped Turgot and influenced Adam Smith's generation. Readers with French meet the school's founder whole. The Tableau alone repays the effort of the language.
the-lights-of-the-church-and-the-light-o:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote his essay as number six in a series on science and Hebrew tradition. He opens by sorting accounts of past events into three classes. A narrative may match what a witness would have seen, may mix truth with error, or may pass into pure fiction.

His example of exact truth is plain. At Whitehall on January 30, 1649, Charles the First lost his head, and no sound witness could doubt what he saw. Details such as speeches, motives, and even the height of the block vary across reports. Huxley uses that test to judge biblical history by evidence rules.
wanderings-in-wessex-an-exploration-of-t:
Edric Holmes, author of Seaward Sussex, wrote Wanderings in Wessex. The book explores the southern realm from Itchen to Otter. It carries twelve full-page drawings by M. M. Vigers. A note at the front states the book's modest aim. No volume of this size could do each place justice, and Holmes offers no apology. His object is only to introduce the would-be traveller to some of the glories of one of England's fairest quarters.

Those glories, he says, are of two kinds. Some are natural beauty. Others are the work of human skill and labor across the centuries. He thanks his predecessors on the high roads and byways of Wessex, who chronicled the history and lore of the countryside before him. Readers get a walking companion to the old kingdom of Wessex.
